reference.source: WHO haematolymphoid classification / paediatric haematology references
clinicalPearls: An aggressive clonal myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm of early childhood
Presents with hepatosplenomegaly, monocytosis, leucocytosis, cytopenias and often a rash
It is driven by dysregulation of the RAS pathway, with mutations in PTPN11, NRAS, KRAS, NF1 or CBL
There are associations with neurofibromatosis type 1 and Noonan syndrome (the latter can cause a self-limiting JMML-like disorder)
Hypersensitivity of myeloid progenitors to granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor is characteristic
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the main curative treatment for most cases
reference.pathophysiology: Juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia arises from constitutive activation of the RAS signal transduction pathway in a haematopoietic stem cell, through mutations in genes such as PTPN11, NRAS, KRAS, NF1 or CBL. This hyperactive signalling makes myeloid progenitors hypersensitive to granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor, driving excessive proliferation of monocytes and granulocytes that infiltrate the spleen, liver, skin and lungs. The clonal proliferation with dysplasia produces the mixed myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative picture and, untreated, is rapidly progressive.
additionalDifferentials: Infection causing reactive monocytosis/hepatosplenomegaly (for example viral)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and film showing monocytosis and immature cells
Bone marrow examination with cytogenetics (including monosomy 7 assessment)
RAS-pathway mutation analysis (PTPN11, NRAS, KRAS, NF1, CBL)
Assessment for neurofibromatosis type 1 and Noonan syndrome
redFlags: Rapidly rising white cell count and organomegaly
Progressive cytopenias with bleeding or infection
reference.prognosis: Untreated JMML is rapidly fatal in most children; allogeneic stem cell transplantation cures many, though relapse occurs, and certain CBL- and Noonan-associated forms may follow a milder or self-resolving course.
pitfalls: Mistaking a viral illness with hepatosplenomegaly for JMML and vice versa
Assuming all RAS-mutant infantile disease is aggressive
management: Proceed to allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as the principal curative treatment for most children
Use cytoreduction such as a hypomethylating agent or low-intensity chemotherapy to control disease burden before transplant
Provide supportive care with blood product transfusion and prompt treatment of infection during the disease course
Consider splenectomy in selected cases for symptomatic splenomegaly or to aid engraftment
Monitor closely for relapse after transplant and manage with donor lymphocyte infusion or second transplantation
Identify NF1 and Noonan syndrome associations and adopt watchful waiting for CBL-mutated and Noonan-associated forms that may self-resolve
Provide genetic counselling and family evaluation for the germline predisposition syndromes
